authority: Regional Authority (Departement WSE / SPW / Bruxelles Économie Emploi) + Immigration Office (DVZ/OE)
form_name: Gecombineerde vergunningsaanvraag / Demande de permis unique
field_label: Single Permit — combined work and residence authorisation
deadline_label: Submit ≥ 4 months before intended start date
non_obvious_official_guidance: Belgium operates a unified 'single permit' covering both the work authorisation (regional competence) and the residence component (federal — DVZ/OE). The employer applies to the competent regional authority, which forwards the file to DVZ/OE once the work authorisation is approved.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The competent region is the region WHERE THE EMPLOYEE WORKS — not where the employer is registered. A Brussels-headquartered employer whose employee works primarily in Ghent must file with the Flemish authority (Departement WSE), not Brussels. Filing with the wrong region causes outright rejection and restarts a 4-month timeline.
non_obvious_action_required: Confirm the primary work location in writing before filing. If the employee will work across regions, use the region where the majority of contracted hours occur. Attach a contract clause specifying work location. Engage a Belgium-licensed immigration lawyer for cross-regional or complex employee profiles.
source: Departement Werk en Sociale Economie (WSE); DVZ / Office des Étrangers (OE)

authority: Belgian Embassy or Consulate in country of legal residence
field_label: Long-stay entry visa (Visa D) — required before travel once single permit is approved
deadline_label: Apply after single-permit approval; allow 3–6 weeks for consular processing
non_obvious_official_guidance: Once DVZ/OE issues the single-permit decision, the non-EEA national must apply for a Visa D at the Belgian embassy or consulate in their country of legal residence before travelling to Belgium.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The Visa D is valid for only 3 months from the date of issue — travel must begin within that window. If the employee's start date is delayed beyond visa validity, a new consular appointment is required. High-backlog nationalities (India, Morocco, Turkey) face 4–8 week waits. Entering Belgium on a Schengen short-stay visa and attempting to regularise from inside is not possible.
non_obvious_action_required: Book the consular appointment the moment the DVZ/OE single-permit decision letter is received. Do not finalise travel arrangements until the Visa D is physically in hand. Build a 6-week consular buffer into start-date planning for high-backlog nationalities. Alert the employee not to depart for Belgium before the visa is issued.
source: FPS Foreign Affairs — Belgian Visa Service

authority: FPS Employment, Labour and Social Dialogue — Limosa system
field_label: Prior posted-worker declaration — mandatory before first working day in Belgium
deadline_label: Submit before employee's first working day in Belgium
non_obvious_official_guidance: Foreign employers seconding workers to Belgium must submit a Limosa-1 declaration via the portal at limosa.be before the worker begins any activity. The worker must carry the L1-acknowledgement document on site at all times.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The Belgian client company must designate a resident 'liaison person' responsible for keeping Limosa documents available for social inspectors. Belgian social inspection conducts unannounced site visits; a missing Limosa triggers immediate work stoppage and joint liability for the client. Limosa does NOT replace immigration status — non-EEA posted workers may simultaneously require a single permit or an exemption certificate. Failing to distinguish these two parallel obligations is a common compliance gap.
non_obvious_action_required: Register on limosa.be and generate the L1 acknowledgement before departure. Print a copy for the employee's work bag. Brief the Belgian client on their liaison obligation in writing before day one. Check whether the employee's nationality and posting duration also triggers a single-permit or exemption requirement — the two systems run in parallel, not instead of each other.
source: FPS Employment, Labour and Social Dialogue — Limosa portal

authority: Private rental market — Flemish Woninghuurdecreet / Walloon Residential Code / Brussels Housing Code
field_label: Housing — rental contract required before commune registration (which requires a Belgian address)
deadline_label: Secure rental contract at least 1 week before arrival to enable commune registration
non_obvious_official_guidance: Belgian rental law is regionalised: the Flemish Woninghuurdecreet, Walloon Residential Tenancy Code, and Brussels Housing Code each govern lease terms, deposit caps (2 months' rent), notice periods, and rent indexation rules separately.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Brussels landlords routinely require 3 months of Belgian payslips, a Belgian bank account, and a Belgian guarantor — none of which a new arrival possesses. This creates a circular dependency: to register at the commune (needed for the bank and rijksregisternummer) you need a permanent address; to get payslips you need to have started work; to open a bank account you need commune registration. The Brussels expat rental market (€1,200–2,200/month for a 1-bed) relies heavily on relocation agencies who pre-screen landlords willing to accept employer guarantee letters in lieu of payslips.
non_obvious_action_required: Prepare an employer guarantee letter on company letterhead before the employee arrives. Engage a relocation agency with Brussels or Antwerp landlord networks. Arrange temporary serviced accommodation for weeks 1–3 to allow commune registration to proceed; commune accepts a temporary address, which breaks the circular dependency. Never expect an employee to navigate this cold without corporate support documentation.
source: Bruxelles Logement; Flandre — Wonen in Vlaanderen; SPW Logement Wallonie

field_label: Arrival declaration — report to commune within 8 working days of establishing residence
deadline_label: Within 8 working days of taking up residence
non_obvious_official_guidance: Any person taking up residence in Belgium must declare their arrival at the commune's population register (registre de la population / bevolkingsregister) within 8 working days.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The commune does not issue the registration certificate immediately. It sends a municipal police officer to physically verify that the employee lives at the declared address — a visit that typically takes 2–6 weeks. Until that visit is completed and logged, the commune cannot issue the Annex 19/8 certificate or initiate the residence card process, and the rijksregisternummer is not generated. Using a hotel or serviced apartment where a concierge may not confirm residency can delay or abort the police visit.
non_obvious_action_required: Declare at the commune in arrival week — do not wait for permanent housing. Ensure the employee will physically be at the declared address when the police officer visits; give the commune a direct mobile number for scheduling. Coordinate with the landlord or building management to expect a police officer. Remind the employee the visit is routine Belgian administrative procedure, not a legal investigation.
source: FPS Home Affairs — Registre national / FOD Binnenlandse Zaken — Nationaal Register

authority: Local commune / gemeente — EU citizen registration desk
field_label: EU/EEA registration — Annex 19 certificate confirming right of residence as employed person
deadline_label: Within 3 months of arrival for stays > 3 months; register in arrival week to start police-visit clock
non_obvious_official_guidance: EU, EEA, and Swiss nationals exercising free movement in Belgium do not need a work permit but must register at the commune if staying longer than 3 months. The commune issues an Annexe 19 (registration certificate) promptly and later an E-card (electronic residence card, valid 5 years) after the police home visit.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The Annexe 19 is typically issued same day or within a few days; the E-card arrives only after the police home visit — 4–8 weeks later. Banks and mutualités increasingly accept the Annexe 19 as interim address proof, but practice varies: KBC and Belfius accept it; some ING branches still require the E-card for non-EEA-origin account holders. Waiting until the 3-month statutory deadline to register delays all downstream steps by weeks.
non_obvious_action_required: Register at the commune as early as possible in arrival week — do not wait near the 3-month limit. Obtain a stamped Annexe 19 at the appointment: this is the operative document for interim bank and insurance onboarding. Present both the Annexe 19 and an employer confirmation letter when approaching the bank to reduce friction caused by the absence of the E-card.
source: FPS Home Affairs — EU citizens' right of residence in Belgium

authority: DVZ / Office des Étrangers — residence card issued via commune
form_name: Electronic residence card type B (single permit holder)
field_label: Electronic residence card (type B) — issued after commune police address verification; required for employment and banking
deadline_label: Initiated by commune post-police visit; card produced in 3–6 weeks
source: DVZ / Office des Étrangers — single permit electronic residence card

authority: Registre national / Nationaal Register — assigned automatically via commune
field_label: National Register Number (rijksregisternummer / numéro de registre national) — 11-digit personal identifier, prerequisite for tax, ONSS, banking, and health insurance
deadline_label: Assigned after commune registration confirmed via police visit; confirm in writing within first month
non_obvious_official_guidance: The 11-digit national register number is automatically assigned to every person formally confirmed in the Belgian population register. It encodes date of birth, sex, and a check digit, and is required for virtually all official interactions in Belgium.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The number is NOT assigned at the time of the commune declaration — it is generated only after the police home visit is completed and the commune formally confirms the registration in the national register (2–6 weeks post-declaration). Until this happens, ONSS/Dimona, mutualité affiliation, tax-on-web access, and bank account opening are all blocked. This single dependency is the most common cause of cascading delays in Belgian onboarding.
non_obvious_action_required: Request written confirmation of the rijksregisternummer from the commune the moment the police visit is logged. Pass the number immediately to HR (for Dimona/ONSS), the mutualité, and the bank. Do not pre-fill forms with a guessed number — it must be the officially assigned value. Follow up proactively with the commune after 3 weeks if not yet confirmed; a single call typically resolves delays.
source: FPS Home Affairs — Registre national / FOD Binnenlandse Zaken — Nationaal Register

authority: Accredited health insurance fund (mutualité / ziekenfonds) — INAMI/RIZIV regulated
field_label: Mutualité / ziekenfonds — mandatory health insurance fund affiliation within 3 months of employment start
deadline_label: Within 3 months of employment start date
non_obvious_official_guidance: All employees in Belgium must affiliate with one of the five accredited funds: CM/MC (Christian, largest), Solidaris (socialist), Mutualité Libérale/Liberale Mutualiteit, Partena/Helan, or the public CAAMI/HZIV. The fund reimburses medical costs at INAMI/RIZIV rates.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Fund choice is irrevocable for the calendar year — employees cannot switch funds between 1 January and 31 December. Supplemental reimbursement rates for dental, optical, physiotherapy, and mental health vary materially between funds. Affiliation requires the rijksregisternummer, so this step is blocked until the commune police visit completes. Missing the 3-month deadline does not trigger a fine but creates a retroactive reimbursement gap from the employment start date.
non_obvious_action_required: Brief the employee on fund differences before arrival so they can decide without time pressure (CM has the widest network; Partena/Helan is popular with expats for multilingual service). Submit affiliation as soon as the rijksregisternummer is confirmed — do not wait for the E-card or residence card. Retain the affiliation certificate for the employer's payroll records.
source: INAMI / RIZIV — health insurance funds in Belgium

authority: Commercial bank (ING, BNP Paribas Fortis, KBC, Belfius, Argenta) — FPS Economy backstop for basic payment service
field_label: Belgian bank account — required for salary payment, direct debits, and utility setup
deadline_label: Open within first month; salary must be paid to a Belgian IBAN for payroll compliance
non_obvious_official_guidance: Belgian law guarantees every resident a basic payment service (service bancaire de base / basisbankdienst). If a commercial bank refuses, the resident may invoke the guarantee mechanism through FPS Economy; the bank has 10 business days to respond.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Non-EEA nationals are frequently declined for standard accounts until both the rijksregisternummer AND a valid residence card are in hand. EEA nationals with an Annexe 19 generally face fewer obstacles. KBC and Belfius are historically more accommodating for new arrivals; ING tends to require the electronic residence card for non-EEA applicants. This creates a salary-payment gap: payroll cannot credit a Belgian IBAN that does not yet exist, and the card may not arrive until week 5–8.
non_obvious_action_required: Attempt opening at KBC or Belfius first, presenting the Annexe 19 or Visa D plus commune declaration receipt as interim documents alongside an employer introductory letter confirming employment and salary. If refused, send a registered letter invoking the basic payment service right — mandatory response in 10 business days. Consider Wise or Revolut as a short-term routing workaround only if the employer payroll system accepts non-Belgian IBANs.
source: FPS Economy — basic payment service (basisbankdienst / service bancaire de base)

authority: ONSS / RSZ (Office national de sécurité sociale / Rijksdienst voor Sociale Zekerheid)
form_name: Dimona (immediate electronic declaration) — employer filing; DmfA quarterly declaration
field_label: Social security registration — employer Dimona before or on first working day; quarterly DmfA thereafter
deadline_label: Dimona: before or on first working day (mandatory); DmfA: quarterly
non_obvious_official_guidance: Employers must file a Dimona (immediate electronic declaration) with ONSS/RSZ before or on each employee's first working day. Quarterly DmfA declarations report hours and remuneration for contribution calculation. Employee contribution: ~13.07% of gross salary; employer contribution: ~27% on top of gross — combined among the highest in the OECD.
non_obvious_actual_reality: For EU/EEA nationals on intra-company transfers or postings, an A1 Certificate from the home-country social security authority exempts the employee from Belgian ONSS — but the A1 must be issued BEFORE the Belgian employment start date. Belgian social inspection rejects retroactive A1 applications without exception. Without an A1, ONSS contributions apply from day one and cannot be reversed. The combined ~40% rate is the single largest cost surprise for employers unfamiliar with Belgian payroll.
non_obvious_action_required: If the employee is posted from an EU/EEA country, apply for the A1 with the home-country social security institution at least 6 weeks before the Belgian start date. File Dimona on or before day one regardless of A1 status — it is a separate, unconditional obligation. For non-EU posted workers, check applicable bilateral social security treaty and obtain a Certificate of Coverage. Engage a Belgian payroll provider for compensation cost-modelling before confirming the employment package.
source: ONSS / RSZ — Dimona and DmfA declarations

authority: SPF Finances / FOD Financiën — Précompte professionnel / Bedrijfsvoorheffing division
form_name: Fiche de rémunération 281.10 / Bezoldigingsfiche; annual withholding-tax circular tables
field_label: Précompte professionnel / bedrijfsvoorheffing — employer withholds personal income tax monthly; expatriate tax regime application window is 3 months
deadline_label: Withheld from first payslip; remitted monthly (large employer) or quarterly; expatriate regime application: within 3 months of start date
non_obvious_official_guidance: Belgian employers withhold bedrijfsvoorheffing from each salary payment under SPF Finances progressive tables (rates up to 50% on income above approximately €46,440/year, 2025 thresholds). The withheld amount is remitted to SPF Finances monthly (large employers) or quarterly (smaller employers).
non_obvious_actual_reality: The expatriate tax regime (Law of 2 April 2021, replacing the old 1983 circular) grants qualifying international hires a 30% tax-free lump-sum expense allowance on salary, capped at €90,000/year. It applies to non-Belgian nationals recruited from abroad or seconded by a foreign group entity. The employer must apply to SPF Finances within 3 months of the employee's start date — no late filing, no retroactive application. The potential annual tax saving is up to €27,000 per year. It is also the most frequently missed high-value administrative act in Belgian onboarding.
non_obvious_action_required: On every international hire, immediately assess eligibility for the expatriate regime: non-Belgian national, recruited from abroad, or seconded by foreign group entity. Engage a Belgian tax adviser before the 3-month window closes — the employer submits the application; the employee cannot apply independently. Once granted, the regime applies until employment ends or the employee moves to a new employer. Document the eligibility assessment even if the regime is declined, for audit readiness.
source: SPF Finances / FOD Financiën — Précompte professionnel; Loi du 2 avril 2021 (régime fiscal des impatriés)

authority: SPF Finances / FOD Financiën — Tax-on-web portal
form_name: Déclaration IPP / Aangifte personenbelasting (PB) — annual personal income tax return
field_label: Annual personal income tax return — filed via Tax-on-web; first-year filers receive no pre-filled form
deadline_label: Annual; online deadline typically 15 July for the preceding tax year
non_obvious_official_guidance: Belgian residents file an annual IPP/PB declaration via Tax-on-web. For established salaried employees, SPF Finances pre-fills the return using employer-declared data. The online filing deadline is typically 15 July; paper deadline is earlier.
non_obvious_actual_reality: First-year filers receive NO pre-filled return — the system has no prior-year data. The employee must file manually and declare all income earned before Belgian tax residency commenced. Belgium taxes residents on worldwide income from the date of commune registration. Foreign-source income (RSUs, pension contributions, dividends, income from prior country) must be declared even if exempt under a double-tax treaty — the exemption is only claimed correctly by declaring and invoking the treaty. First-year returns are among the most common audit triggers for international employees.
non_obvious_action_required: Engage a Belgian tax adviser for the employee's first filing year without exception. Confirm the tax residency start date (generally the date of commune registration confirmation). Identify all applicable double-tax treaties for foreign-source income streams. For expatriate regime holders, the adviser must calculate the correct taxable base under the regime for the first partial year — the standard pre-fill does not handle this. Do not leave first-year filing to the employee unaided.
source: SPF Finances / FOD Financiën — Tax-on-web; Belgian IPP/PB legislation

authority: Local commune + DVZ / Office des Étrangers
form_name: Single permit renewal application (employer-initiated, via commune)
field_label: Single permit and residence card renewal — employer must initiate 3–4 months before card expiry; employee enters irregular status if card lapses
deadline_label: Submit renewal 3–4 months before expiry; calendar reminder at 5 months for operational buffer
non_obvious_official_guidance: Single permits (type B card) expire after 1 year on initial grant or up to 3 years on renewal for stable employment. The employer initiates renewal with the competent regional authority 3 months before expiry; DVZ/OE processes the residential component in parallel.
non_obvious_actual_reality: DVZ/OE renewal processing takes 4–6 months in practice despite a 4-month statutory target. If filed on time (≥ 3 months before expiry), the commune issues an attestation d'immatriculation / attest van immatriculatie that functions as a valid residence and work authorisation during processing — the employee may continue working lawfully. If the application is filed late and the card lapses before the receipt is issued, the employee enters an irregular status gap; employers have been audited and fined for employing workers during such gaps.
non_obvious_action_required: Set the calendar reminder at 5 months before expiry (not 3) to build in processing buffer. The employer must initiate both components simultaneously: the regional work-authorisation renewal and the DVZ/OE residential renewal. Verify that the employee's role, salary, and work location are unchanged since the last permit — any material change may require a new single permit application rather than a renewal, triggering the full 4-month process again.
source: DVZ / Office des Étrangers — single permit renewal
